newsitem.title: USA: SEC steps up probe of central California bond deal.
newsitem.headline: SEC steps up probe of central California bond deal.

text.p: The Securities and Exchange Commission has subpoenaed information about a central California bond issue six months after state Treasurer Matt Fong called on the SEC to investigate the deal's underwriter.

People involved in the investigation said the SEC subpoenaed documents about nearly $17 million of bonds issued by the Sierra Central Valley Public Financing Authority and underwritten by San Francisco-based Pacific Genesis Group Inc. The SEC has also interviewed officials involved in the deal.

The subpoenas and interviews were the first indications to date that the SEC was actively following up on Fong's request for a federal investigation of several bond transactions involving Pacific Genesis Group.
An SEC official declined to comment Thursday.

Pacific Genesis Group was not immediately available to comment on the developments. Last year, the firm said it hoped to meet with the SEC to "clear up any misconceptions coming from the treasurer's office."

In mid-March, the SEC subpoenaed documents about the Sierra Central Valley deal from the San Joaquin River Parkway and Conservation Trust, a California non-profit corporation that buys land along the river, according to the trust's general counsel, Christopher Brown.
He said the trust was asked to provide the SEC with documents relating to a property in Madera County that was part of the Sierra Central Valley authority deal.
The authority issued nearly $17 million of notes in December 1995 to buy land for a golf course project, a casino and for other purposes. An Indian tribe took part in the deal.
The San Joaquin River Parkway trust had been approached by the land developer to participate in the deal. But after studying the proposal, it chose not to take part, Brown said.

On March 31, the trust's executive director, Dave Koehler, was deposed by the SEC in Fresno, California. During that interview, the SEC focused on the valuation of the property and on other land use issues related to the deal, Brown said.
The SEC launched its investigation of the Sierra Central Valley deal following Fong's request for an inquiry, people involved in the case said.
Last September, Fong called for the SEC and the state's Attorney General to investigate several projects underwritten by Pacific Genesis, including the Sierra Central Valley deal.
In these deals, Fong alleged that illegal payments of bond proceeds were made, and that bond proceeds were used to retire private debts.

In some of these transactions, Fong alleged that Indian tribes were represented to be the local agencies on whose behalf the bonds were issued even though Indian tribes are not eligible to participate in these types of deals.

The transactions were conducted under the state's so-called Marks-Roos Local Bond Pooling Act, which allows certain types of local government agencies to form joint powers authorities to finance capital projects.
In recent years, bonds issued under the Marks-Roos bond act have been the subject of several state and federal investigations and a source of controversy in Sacramento.
Later this month, California state lawmakers will debate a bill that would clear the way for Indian tribes to participate in Marks-Roos bond transactions.
Assembly Bill 229, by Republican Assemblyman Jim Battin, would amend the Marks-Roos bond act to expand the definition of local agency to include federally recognized Indian tribes.
The state Assembly Committee on Local Government is expected to consider the measure at its meeting on April 16.
